nt: וִ⁠יהוֹרָ֣ם בֶּן־אַחְאָ֗ב מָלַ֤ךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ בְּ⁠שֹׁ֣מְר֔וֹן בִּ⁠שְׁנַת֙ שְׁמֹנֶ֣ה עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לִ⁠יהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה וַ⁠יִּמְלֹ֖ךְ שְׁתֵּים־עֶשְׂרֵ֥ה שָׁנָֽה

In this verse and the next two verses, the author is introducing **Jehoram** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Israel**. In the preceding book of 1 Kings, the author introduced each new king in this same way, and he will introduce each new king this way throughout this book. It would be good to show this in your translation by representing his characteristic phrases the same way each time. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated these phrases in [1 Kings 15:1](../1ki/15/01.md) and similar instances throughout that book.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **18**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat’s reign]

The author is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean things of a certain kind. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [evil things] or [what was evil]

nt: The author is speaking of Jehoram continuing to do sinful things as if he had **clung** to them physically. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Since the pronoun **it** refers back to the **sins** of Jeroboam, it may be more natural in your language to use a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [He did not turn away from them]

The author is speaking of Jehoram’s continuing sins as if they were something he could have turned away from physically. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He did not stop committing them] or [He did not abandon them]

nt: In this context, the author does not mean that Jehoram **went** somewhere. He means that he took the action that he describes next. Alternate translation: [And he took action]

See the discussion of this term in the Introduction to 2 Kings. In contexts such as this, it introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly, here or in its other instances in the book.
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:3](../01/03.md). Alternate translation: [I will go]
כָּמ֧וֹ⁠נִי כָמ֛וֹ⁠ךָ כְּ⁠עַמִּ֥⁠י כְ⁠עַמֶּ֖⁠ךָ כְּ⁠סוּסַ֥⁠י כְּ⁠סוּסֶֽי⁠ךָ

Jehoshaphat is using a common expression of his culture to agree to join Jehoram in an attack against Moab. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in [1 Kings 22:4](../1ki/22/04.md), where Jehoshaphat says the same thing to Jehoram’s father Ahab. Alternate translation: [I and my army with its horses will fight alongside you and your army with its horses]

nt: The pronoun **he** refers to Jehoram in the first instance in this verse, while it refers to Jehoshaphat in the second instance. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Jehoram said … And Jehoshaphat replied]

Jehoram is using **Where is this, the way we shall go up** as a common expression of his culture to ask what **way** or route they should take. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By what way should we go up]

nt: The author assumes that readers will understand that by **they went around**, he means that these armies went around the southern end of the Dead Sea. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. You may wish to use the name that this body of water had in biblical times, “the Sea of the Arabah.” Alternate translation: [and they went around the Dead Sea] or [and they went around the Sea of the Arabah]

Here, **the camp** represents the soldiers who were camped there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the soldiers]

The author is using the expression **at their feet** to represent that these **animals** were walking behind the soldiers as they marched. As [3:16](../03/16.md) suggests, these probably included cattle to eat, horses to ride into battle, and animals to carry supplies. Alternate translation: [that were walking behind them]

If not, you could say what the king of Israel was feeling, or you could say what made him distressed. Alternate translation: [What a disaster] or [This makes me distressed]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [It certainly appears that]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 13. Alternate translation: [into the power of Moab]

וַ⁠יֵּרְד֣וּ אֵלָ֗י⁠ו מֶ֧לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל וִ⁠יהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט וּ⁠מֶ֥לֶךְ אֱדֽוֹם

The tents of these kings were probably on a height overlooking the camp of their soldiers, while Elisha was probably staying down within the camp. The author is marking travel for change in elevation. See how you translated the comparable expression “go up” in [1:3](../01/03.md). Alternate translation: [And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went to him]

x.ASV: And Elisha said unto the king of Israel, What have I to do with thee? get thee to the prophets of thy father, and to the prophets of thy mother. And the king of Israel said unto him, Nay; for Jehovah hath called these three kings together to deliver them into the hand of Moab.
x.Darby: And Elisha said to the king of Israel, What have I to do with thee? go to the prophets of thy father and to the prophets of thy mother. And the king of Israel said to him, Not so, for Jehovah has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab.
x.KJV: And Elisha said unto the king of Israel, What have I to do with thee? get thee to the prophets of thy father, and to the prophets of thy mother. And the king of Israel said unto him, Nay: for the Lord hath called these three kings together, to deliver them into the hand of Moab.
x.YLT: And Elisha saith unto the king of Israel, `What--to me and to thee? go unto the prophets of thy father, and unto the prophets of thy mother;' and the king of Israel saith to him, `Nay, for Jehovah hath called for these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab.'

nt: Elisha is using **What to me and to you** as a common expression of his culture to insist that he has nothing in common with the **king of Israel** when it comes to seeking divine guidance. As Elisha notes, King Jehoram worships Baal, and so Elisha says he should ask prophets of Baal to help him rather than a prophet of Yahweh. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the same expression in [2 Samuel 16:10](../2sa/16/10.md). Alternate translation: [I want to have nothing to do with your request that I seek divine guidance for you!]

Elisha actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying. He does not actually want the king of Israel to consult false prophets. Rather, he is rebuking him for his idolatry. If, for such a purpose, a speaker of your language would not say the opposite of what he meant, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You had no right to come to me, since you and your family worship false gods]

x.Darby: And Elisha said, As Jehovah of hosts liveth, before whom I stand, surely, were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would not look toward thee nor see thee.
x.KJV: And Elisha said, As the Lord of hosts liveth, before whom I stand, surely, were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would not look toward thee, nor see thee.
x.YLT: And Elisha saith, `Jehovah of Hosts liveth, before whom I have stood; for unless the face of Jehoshaphat king of Judah I am lifting up, I do not look unto thee, nor see thee;

nt: חַי־יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָמַ֣דְתִּי לְ⁠פָנָ֔י⁠ו כִּ֗י לוּלֵ֛י פְּנֵ֛י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֖ה אֲנִ֣י נֹשֵׂ֑א אִם־אַבִּ֥יט אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אִם־אֶרְאֶֽ⁠ךָּ

Following the custom of his culture, Elisha is swearing an oath by guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred and by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. In a context such as this, it may be natural to express just the first part of the condition as a negative statement. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh of hosts, to whose face I stand, that unless I were lifting the face of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, I would not look at you and I would not regard you]

Here, **to whose face I stand** represents being in the presence of Yahweh and serving him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in whose presence I stand] or [whose servant I am]
לוּלֵ֛י פְּנֵ֛י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֖ה אֲנִ֣י נֹשֵׂ֑א אִם־אַבִּ֥יט אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אִם־אֶרְאֶֽ⁠ךָּ

If it would appear in your language that Elisha was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [I am only looking at you and regarding you because I am lifting the face of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah]

Elisha is using **lifting the face of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “showing respect to” or “showing favor toward.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if I did not respect Jehoshaphat]

Elisha is saying he would actually not even **look at** or **regard** the king of Israel. He means that he would not do the slightest thing to help him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I would not do the slightest thing to help you]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I would not even look at you at all]
